questions.question: What is biodiversity? Why is biodiversity important for human lives?
answer_steps: Biodiversity is the variety of life forms, plants, animals and micro-organisms, that live in a habitat and are interdependent.
Plants, animals and micro-organisms recreate the quality of the air we breathe, the water we drink and the soil that produces our food.
Forests are primary producers; biodiversity gives us food, medicine (like taxol from the Himalayan yew), timber and genetic diversity for crops and fisheries, and keeps the ecosystem balanced.

questions.question: How have human activities affected the depletion of flora and fauna? Explain.
answer_steps: Colonial railways, agriculture, commercial forestry and mining destroyed forests; between 1951 and 1980 over 26,200 sq km of forest was converted to farmland.
Monoculture plantations (teak, chir pine), river valley projects (over 5,000 sq km cleared since 1951) and mining (dolomite in Buxa) destroyed habitats.
Hunting, poaching, over-exploitation, pollution and forest fires have pushed many species to the threatened list.

questions.question: Describe how communities have conserved and protected forests and wildlife in India.
answer_steps: In Sariska Tiger Reserve, Rajasthan, villagers fought against mining by citing the Wildlife Protection Act.
In Alwar district, five villages declared 1,200 hectares as the Bhairodev Dakav 'Sonchuri', with their own rules banning hunting and keeping out encroachers.
The Chipko movement in the Himalayas resisted deforestation and showed the success of community afforestation with indigenous species.
Through Joint Forest Management (from 1988, first in Odisha), village institutions protect degraded forests and share non-timber produce and timber.
Sacred groves, worship of trees like mahua, kadamba, peepal and banyan, and Bishnoi villages protecting blackbuck, nilgai and peacocks preserve nature through tradition.

questions.question: Write a note on good practices towards conserving forest and wildlife.
answer_steps: The Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 banned hunting, restricted wildlife trade and set up national parks and sanctuaries.

Special projects protect the tiger (Project Tiger, 1973), one-horned rhino, Kashmir stag, three types of crocodiles and the Asiatic lion; insects (1980, 1986) and plants (1991) were added to the protected list.
Joint Forest Management involves villagers in restoring degraded forests in return for a share of produce.
Beej Bachao Andolan and Navdanya show diversified farming without synthetic chemicals is possible.
Community efforts like Chipko, the Alwar sonchuri and sacred groves protect forests; conservation now focuses on whole biodiversity rather than a few species.

questions.question: Distinguish between endangered and endemic species, with one example each.

questions.question: How does the loss of forests and wildlife affect people?
answer_steps: It causes a loss of cultural diversity, since many indigenous communities depend on forests for food, medicine, culture and spirituality.

Deforestation leads to droughts and floods, which hurt the poor most.

questions.question: What were the main features of Project Tiger?
answer_steps: It was launched in 1973 when tiger numbers had fallen from about 55,000 to 1,827.
It aimed to protect tigers from poaching, loss of habitat and depletion of prey.
Tiger reserves like Corbett, Sunderbans, Bandhavgarh, Sariska, Manas and Periyar were set up; it preserves whole biotypes, not just one species.

questions.question: Explain the major causes of the depletion of forests and wildlife in India.
answer_steps: Colonial expansion of railways, agriculture, commercial and scientific forestry, and mining caused the greatest damage.
Agricultural expansion converted over 26,200 sq km of forest between 1951 and 1980; shifting cultivation degraded tribal belts.
Enrichment plantations of single species like teak and chir pine replaced natural forests.
Development projects (over 5,000 sq km for river valley projects; Narmada Sagar would drown 40,000 ha) and mining (dolomite in Buxa) destroyed habitats.
Hunting, poaching, over-exploitation, pollution, poisoning, forest fires, and unequal consumption by the rich add to the damage.

questions.question:
Read the source and answer the questions.

*"In India joint forest management (JFM) programme furnishes a good example for involving local communities in the management and restoration of degraded forests. The programme has been in formal existence since 1988 when the state of Odisha passed the first resolution for joint forest management."* (NCERT)

(i) Which state passed the first resolution for JFM? (1)

(ii) What kind of forest land does JFM mostly work on? (1)

(iii) How do local communities benefit from JFM, and why does this help conservation? (2)
answer_steps: (i) Odisha, in 1988.
(ii) Degraded forest land managed by the Forest Department.
(iii) Members get intermediary benefits like non-timber forest produce and a share in the timber harvested; since they gain from healthy forests, they protect them.
